Using high-speed cameras, experts have solved the mystery behind the typical squeaking of sneakers in sports halls. Many people know that sneakers squeak on wood or plastic - the exact mechanism remained unclear for a long time. "What happens between the shoe and the floor is very complex. Experimentally proving exactly where the squeak comes from is therefore extremely difficult," explains the Dutch friction researcher Bart Weber from the Advanced Research Center for Nanolithography (ARCNL) in conversation with ORF Wissen.

In a recently published Study An international research team was able to solve this puzzle in the journal “Nature”. The experts used high-speed cameras to film basketball shoes sliding across a glass plate.

expect.header: Swinging sole: Waves instead of smooth gliding
expect.bodytext:
The video recordings show: The shoes do not glide evenly over the smooth surface. Instead, the soles deform; Wave-like impulses arise that spread across the contact surface. “Like waves that arrive on the beach, similar waves also travel through the sole of the shoe,” says Weber. "With each wave, the shoe moves a tiny fraction of a millimeter further. And this happens very quickly: the waves race across the ground at up to 300 kilometers per hour."

Weber himself was not directly involved in the research team's experiments, but he has long been interested in friction between different objects and wrote an article accompanying the study in the journal "Nature". According to him, it is precisely these waves in the soles of shoes that are responsible for the typical squeaking noise. The sole begins to vibrate in a certain rhythm - comparable to a tuning fork - and is heard as a high-frequency sound. Each sole has a preferred vibration frequency based on thickness, mass and stiffness. For the basketball shoes examined in the study, it was around 5,000 Hertz.

expect.header: When does squeaking occur? Speed ​​and surface
expect.bodytext:
The pitch of the squeak does not depend on how quickly the shoe slides across the surface. It is primarily determined by the mechanical properties of the sole.

However, the sliding speed determines whether a squeak occurs at all: only from a minimum speed - the so-called critical sliding speed – the sound becomes audible. For sneakers, this threshold is typically around one meter per second.

The research team also compared materials and surfaces: Smooth rubber surfaces produced rather irregular pulses and therefore no clear high-frequency tones. Structured surfaces - such as the profile of sports shoes - led to consistent pulse frequencies and thus the characteristic squeaking.

expect.header: More than basketball: a universal phenomenon
expect.bodytext:
The researchers showed that they could influence the frequency or pitch of the squeak by specifically changing material properties and surface structures. According to Weber, this could have practical uses: The principle of swinging soles is probably not limited to basketball shoes.

“If you drive your car through a garage with a very clean, smooth floor and make a turn, you hear the same noise – probably from the same mechanism.” The squeaking sound when a finger passes over a balloon or the sound of squeaking bicycle brakes are probably based on the same principle.

“I really hope that this basic understanding will help us in the future to specifically prevent squeaking where we don’t want it – or to increase it where we need it,” says Weber. Where brakes squeak, it is often annoying; In the sports hall, however, acoustic feedback can help you orient yourself on the field - targeted reinforcement could even make sense there.

The last light lies golden on the rooftops,
the chestnut trees wear fresh, bright leaves.
From an open window comes a laugh,
and blossom dust still lies on the pavement.

I walk slowly through the warm air:
a neighbour says hello, then a song from far away.
It is the small things that stay with us,
as quiet and certain as the first star.

Then it grows dark, little by little,
the blackbird sings once more, then all is still.
Spring holds on to the evening
and covers the city with a gentle breath.

set.title: Local Easter egg hunt: all places taken
set.teaser: All places for this weekend’s egg hunt are taken. The team is therefore planning extra search areas and stations with clues in pastel colours.
set.bodytext:
The annual Easter egg hunt on the village green has a record number of sign-ups. So the team is splitting the hunt into separate rounds: for young children, for families and for older participants. That way each group has enough space.

Volunteers spent the whole week preparing markers, baskets and surprise stations. Local cafés and shops are opening longer and will welcome visitors after the first round in the morning.

set.title: Natural egg dyes: a second workshop date
set.teaser: The first workshop on dyeing eggs with natural colours was fully booked within a few hours. Now there is a second date.
set.bodytext:
More and more families dye their Easter eggs with natural colours. The workshop uses onion skins, turmeric, beetroot and herbs. The course leaders show how soft shades and patterns build up in several layers.

Everyone takes their finished eggs home. There is also a short guide and ideas for a spring table with little waste. You can repeat the techniques at home over the Easter weekend.

set.title: Painted eggs at the centre of the table
set.teaser: Local designers show how a few painted eggs can decorate a spring table. It does not need heavy decoration.
set.bodytext:
This year’s trend: clear arrangements, small flowers and groups of eggs in matching colours. The table should not look full. A few well-chosen details set the mood.

Soft pink, cream, yellow and pale green are the most popular colours. Ceramic bowls and linen table runners go well with them. This is easy to copy at home, for brunch or lunch over the holidays.

set.title: Speckled chocolate eggs are in demand
set.teaser: Shops report high demand for speckled chocolate eggs. Many people buy eggs from small makers and boxes with mixed colours.
set.bodytext:
Small confectioners report that customers are looking for Easter sweets that look playful and make good gifts. Speckled mini eggs sell best. They fit in baskets, on the table and with desserts.

Some shops add handwritten cards or small bunches of flowers. That turns a simple purchase into a spring gift. Retailers expect even more customers in the week before Easter.

set.title: Rows of pastel eggs fill the shop windows
set.teaser: Many shop windows in town show neat rows of pastel eggs at Easter. This looks lighter and more graphic than a window full of decoration.
set.bodytext:
According to the shops, customers respond well to clear colour patterns and tidy displays. Instead of filling every corner, many windows show repeated egg shapes, simple paper backgrounds and only a few flowers.

This keeps the decoration modern, and the familiar Easter symbols stay visible. Designers describe the style as cheerful and easy to read from the street. It suits small shops with little space for decoration.

set.title: Classic Easter baskets are back
set.teaser: Florists and home shops are selling more nest-style baskets again. They are filled with eggs, ribbons and fresh greenery.
set.bodytext:
After a few years of eye-catching decoration, many households are going back to classic Easter decoration. Baskets with eggs, ribbons and fresh greenery are especially popular. They serve as a gift and as table decoration at the same time.

Retailers report that customers like warm, familiar decoration that does not feel too formal. Traditional decoration still appeals to many people if it stays simple and balanced.

set.title: Photo series: Easter eggs in morning light
set.teaser: A new photo series shows Easter eggs outdoors. Grass and morning light create a calm spring mood.
set.bodytext:
The series is shared often because it uses simple means and natural backgrounds. Instead of staged indoor scenes, the photographer uses grass, shadows and open space. This makes the eggs look fresh and light.

Viewers like the calm tone of the pictures. They connect Easter customs with the start of spring. Several local clubs now use similar ideas for their own announcements and invitations.

set.title: Painted faces make eggs personal
set.teaser: In craft classes, eggs with painted faces are popular with children and adults. A simple smile is enough.
set.bodytext:
This style needs only a few materials, and every egg gets its own character. Course leaders say it works well for mixed age groups. Depending on the time available, the designs stay simple or become more detailed.

Parents like that the finished eggs get people talking at brunch or on family visits. The trend combines humour with tradition. You do not need any painting skills for it.

set.title: Pastel shades set the tone for Easter brunch
set.teaser: Light blue, soft pink, mint and cream shape the tables at Easter brunch. The eggs set the colours.
set.bodytext:
Pastel eggs can be the basis for a whole holiday colour scheme without buying much that is new. Once the eggs are chosen, napkins, flowers and crockery follow in the same shade.

This works especially well for daytime gatherings, when daylight makes the colours look fresh. Hosts like tables that are festive and still calm. That keeps even a long brunch pleasant.

set.title: A circle of eggs as a centrepiece
set.teaser: Stylists recommend round arrangements of eggs for the Easter table. Such circles look balanced and suit any size of table.
set.bodytext:
A circle of eggs works through repetition, with little effort. Often six or eight eggs are placed around a candle, a small vase or a serving plate. This turns ordinary tableware into an eye-catcher.

The format suits a large lunch as well as a small family breakfast. After the meal you can keep using the eggs: on a shelf, in a basket or in the window.

set.title: Egg hunt: a longer route for young children
set.teaser: The team has extended the route for the youngest age group. This means more children can look for eggs calmly and with plenty of space.
set.bodytext:
Feedback from recent years shows that young children enjoy the hunt more when it is calm and the search area is safe. Volunteers have therefore widened the paths and hung the signs lower. There are shaded resting places along the route.

Parents welcomed the changes during visits beforehand and expect a relaxed morning for everyone. The change is part of a larger plan to make local spring festivals easier for families.

set.title: Dyeing recipes from school for the holidays
set.teaser: Teachers give children short guides to dyeing eggs with natural colours to take home. Families can continue the Easter projects during the holidays.
set.bodytext:
The guides use cheap materials and short steps. Children can follow them with help from an adult. The idea came from lessons, where simple colour experiments quickly became a popular spring activity.

By handing out the recipes before the holidays, teachers want to give families a quiet indoor activity. Parents have responded well to craft ideas that connect school and Easter customs.

set.title: Eggs from above: photos for the spring menu
set.teaser: Restaurants and cafés show tidy photos of eggs taken from above. They use them to announce their Easter specials on menus and in posts.
set.bodytext:
Creative teams say photos of eggs work because people recognise them at once. The pictures also suit very different brand styles. Some choose bright shots for playful brunch offers, others muted tones for elegant holiday menus.

The format works well online too, because simple pictures stay readable on small screens. Many restaurants now advertise their Easter week mainly with a few carefully arranged eggs.

set.title: Small gift boxes built around mini eggs
set.teaser: In many shop displays, gift boxes with small Easter eggs are replacing larger novelty items.
set.bodytext:
Retailers see that customers prefer smaller gifts that feel thoughtful but not excessive. Mini eggs fit well in boxes with tea, candles, biscuits or handwritten cards.

The eggs add colour and show at once that it is Easter. So the rest of the packaging can stay simple. The trend shows a practical way of giving that still has charm.

set.title: Shop windows: repetition instead of abundance
set.teaser: At Easter this year, many shop windows show repeated egg shapes instead of a lot of decoration.
set.bodytext:
Design studios explain that repeated shapes are easy to recognise from a distance and give the window a clear rhythm. Easter eggs are well suited to this. They stand for the season at once and are abstract enough for modern layouts.

The simple style also saves time when setting up. That helps smaller shops that run several promotions at once. The result is practical and still looks fresh and festive.

set.title: Hand-woven Easter baskets in early demand
set.teaser: Sellers of handmade baskets at local markets report a good start to the season. Customers are preparing egg hunts, gifts and the spring table.
set.bodytext:
According to the market stalls, the first Easter customers are looking for sturdy baskets for several uses. A basket is used for the egg hunt in the morning and later stands on the table. After the holidays it is used for storage.

This versatility makes woven baskets especially popular this year. Sellers expect good demand until the last weekend before Easter. The better weather forecast also helps.

set.title: Eggs outdoors give Easter photos more texture
set.teaser: Photographers are moving their egg shoots outdoors. There, grass, shadows and spring light look more natural.
set.bodytext:
Outdoor shots give Easter pictures more depth without elaborate props. Grass, moss and uneven light add texture to the picture. This makes simple eggs look livelier in articles and on social media.

The style especially helps local clubs that promote egg hunts, workshops and markets. A simple outdoor scene often shows spring better than an elaborately staged studio shot.

set.title: Character eggs are back at the craft table
set.teaser: Eggs with faces, ears and small accessories are back. The idea is simple and appeals to children and parents.
set.bodytext:
According to the craft teams, the format sparks the imagination, and families do not need special tools. Felt-tip pens, paper and a few leftover pieces of ribbon are often enough. These become rabbits, chicks or funny little figures.

The finished eggs are easy to photograph. That is why you often see them on school walls, in family albums and on Easter cards. Because the idea is simple and fun, it stays popular year after year.

set.title: Soft colours shape Easter decoration
set.teaser: Designers still start their Easter decoration with calm pastel eggs. Loud contrasts are less in demand.
set.bodytext:
When eggs are the starting point for a room or a table, the rest of the decoration often becomes simpler. Two to four shades are enough to look festive and still go together.

You can now see this approach in home decoration, bakery packaging, invitations and at brunch. The egg remains the clearest symbol. But it is the choice of colours that makes the decoration last.

set.title: Round arrangements for small Easter tables
set.teaser: Compact circles of eggs help to make small Easter tables look festive.
set.bodytext:
Not every table has room for a large arrangement. That is why round arrangements are catching on. The eggs lie around a single plate, a vase or a cake stand, and the table still looks well planned.

Hosts like that the eggs can be arranged quickly with things from their own household. A festive Easter mood often comes from arrangement and colour rather than quantity.
